newsitem.title: USA: U.S. in rearguard action to save Middle East peace.
newsitem.headline: U.S. in rearguard action to save Middle East peace.

text.p: The United States, which just a few months ago was leading the push for a comprehensive Middle East peace, is now fighting a desperate rearguard action to prevent the peace process crumbling altogether.

The summit of Israeli and Arab leaders that the White House has called on Tuesday after bloody Israeli-Palestinian clashes in the West Bank last week is a symptom of how far the Middle East malaise that began last spring has deteriorated.

Until now, it had been the proud boast of the U.S. administration that Israel and the Palestinians had their own negotiating track and did not need American intervention other than to organise aid for the self-rule Palestinian Authority.

The crisis sparked by Israel's decision to open a tunnel for tourists near the al-Aqsa mosque in Arab East Jerusalem has dramatically demonstrated how fragile that track is, with the two sides unable to agree on a meeting by themselves.

While the immediate U.S. aim is to stop the fighting and get Israelis and Palestinians talking again, the larger objective is "to prevent the unravelling of the whole Oslo process," said Stanley Roth of the U.S. Institute of Peace.
The Oslo agreement of 1993 set in train Palestinian self-rule in the West Bank and Gaza Strip and opened the way for agreements between Israel and her other Arab neighbours.

Analysts are not the only doom-sayers. British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind warned last week of "a very deep deterioration in the peace process with a very real danger that the peace process could be on the verge of collapse".

In this situation, a major success would be just to follow through on accords already reached such as for Israeli troops to pull out of the West Bank town of Hebron, and Israelis and Palestinians to pursue talks on thorny issues like Jerusalem.
More ambitious objectives have had to be shelved for now.

For a few fleeting weeks at the beginning of this year, U.S. mediators believed Syria was about to strike an agreement with Israel's former Labour government that would ultimately lead to most Arab countries recognising the Jewish state.

It was not to be. A string of Islamic truck bombings in Israel, an iron-fisted Israeli response to guerrilla attacks from Lebanon, and the election defeat of Labour Prime Minister Shimon Peres by right-winger Benjamin Netanyahu sent events in a sharply different direction.
Netanyahu has stalled on talks with the Palestinians and said he will not return the Golan Heights to Syria.
While Washington continues to try to interest Syria in resuming negotiations, even U.S. officials admit there is no prospect of that happening any time soon.
Some U.S. analysts believe the peace process has, in any case, gone too far too fast and needs to slow down.

"It may help to think of Middle East peace over the past five years as a stock whose price has soared: a correction is inevitable," said Richard Haass, Middle East adviser to former President George Bush.

"The goal of American diplomacy ought to be to minimise the size of the correction and avoid giving back all the hard-earned gains," Haass wrote in the latest edition of the authoritative journal "Foreign Affairs".

Warren Christopher, the ever-hopeful U.S. Secretary of State who has made Middle East peace his top personal priority, has conceded that "this is the most serious situation since the series of four deadly bombings in Israel."
But, he said, "the peace process survived that and has survived other threats to it."
Keeping it alive, however, has required a difficult decision by President Bill Clinton to become personally involved at a critical time in his campaign for the U.S. November 5 presidential election.

Some U.S. officials said privately that Clinton was taking a considerable risk by bringing the Middle East protagonists and their bitter quarrels to the forefront of the U.S. political stage in Washington.

Clinton may have calculated that the pledges to have a fresh stab at reviving peace talks that can be expected from this week's summit, while they may not help him, may not harm him either in a campaign focused largely on domestic affairs.
Domestic fallout from the U.S. foreign policy setback in northern Iraq, where intervention by Baghdad last month effectively ended Washington's influence in the area, appears to have been minimal.
And some U.S. analysts believe the Arab-Israeli peace process can recover in the long run, given the lack of superpower rivalry in the region that bedevilled peace efforts during the Cold War.
"The situation is far from hopeless," Roth said. "Sometimes things have to get sufficiently bad to prod a process forward."
